title: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE NEVER HEARD JESUS SPEAK?
paragraphs:
“MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE NEVER HEARD JESUS SPEAK?
What John 10:27 Really Means, How Christ Leads His People, and Why Every Christian Must Learn the Difference Between the Shepherd’s Voice and the Voices Inside Their Own Head
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that has comforted millions of Christians.
It has also quietly terrified some of them.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27
Beautiful words.
Until you are sitting alone at two in the morning, Bible open, heart exhausted, asking a question you are almost ashamed to admit:
“Jesus… if I am really one of Your sheep, why can’t I hear You?”
Maybe you have watched other Christians say things with astonishing confidence.
“God told me.”
“The Lord spoke to me.”
“Jesus said this was the person I should marry.”
“God told me to quit.”
“God told me to move.”
“God gave me a word for you.”
And somewhere underneath your polite smile, another thought appeared.
What about me?
Why does God apparently speak so clearly to everyone else?
Maybe you prayed.
You waited.
You listened.
Nothing.
No audible voice.
No supernatural whisper.
No sentence suddenly appearing inside your mind.
Just silence.
And eventually the silence began accusing you.
Maybe my faith is weak.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
Maybe I am spiritually deaf.
Maybe I am not actually one of His sheep.
But what if the problem is not that Jesus has abandoned you?
What if part of the problem is that Christians sometimes use the phrase “hearing God’s voice” in ways that are much broader than the way Jesus is using it in John 10?
Because when Jesus said,
“My sheep hear my voice,”
He was not handing Christians a technique for receiving secret messages.
He was revealing something infinitely deeper.
He was revealing the relationship between the Shepherd and the people He saves.
And when you understand what Jesus actually said, one of the most confusing phrases in modern Christianity becomes one of the most beautiful promises in the Gospel.
The Greek text of John 10:27 reads:
“Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.”
Transliterated:
Ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin, kagō ginōskō auta, kai akolouthousin moi.
“My sheep hear/listen to My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.”
Notice the movement.
My sheep.
My voice.
I know them.
They follow Me.
Jesus is describing belonging, recognition, relationship, and discipleship.
The Greek verb translated “hear” is ἀκούω — akouō.
It can mean to hear, listen to, or pay attention to what is spoken. Context determines the nuance.
And the context matters enormously.
Jesus had already painted the picture earlier in the chapter.
“The sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.” — John 10:3
Then:

“And when he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him: for they know his voice. And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers.” — John 10:4–5
Jesus is using shepherd imagery.
The sheep belong to the shepherd.
They recognize the shepherd.
They trust the shepherd.
They follow the shepherd.
And then Jesus takes the metaphor somewhere breathtaking.
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11
Suddenly the passage is no longer primarily about your ability to detect spiritual impressions.
It is about Jesus.
The Shepherd.
The One who knows His sheep.
The One whose sheep belong to Him.
The One whose sheep recognize and follow Him.
And ultimately…
the Shepherd who dies for them.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity does not begin with your ability to hear God.
Christianity begins with a God who came looking for sinners.
You were not wandering through the wilderness successfully tuning your spiritual frequency until you finally discovered Jesus.
Jesus came for the lost.
Jesus called sinners.
Jesus laid down His life.
Jesus rose again.
Jesus saves.
And His sheep respond to their Shepherd.
But there is another detail in John 10 that makes Christ’s statement even more powerful.
Immediately before verse 27, some of the Jewish leaders demand:
“If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.” — John 10:24
Jesus responds:
“I told you, and ye believed not.” — John 10:25
Then He says:
“But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep.” — John 10:26
And only then:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27
The immediate contrast is not between Christians who receive private revelations and Christians who do not.
The contrast is between unbelief and the people who recognize, receive, and follow Jesus.
They were standing physically close enough to hear Jesus’ audible voice.
Their ears worked perfectly.
Yet they did not believe.
That should stop us.
Because apparently a human being can hear the sound of Jesus’ physical voice…
and still fail to truly “hear” the Shepherd.
So whatever John 10:27 means, it cannot simply mean detecting audible sound.
There is a deeper hearing.
A hearing that receives Christ.
A hearing that recognizes Him for who He is.
A hearing that produces following.
Jesus says something similar elsewhere:
“He that is of God heareth God’s words.” — John 8:47
And again:
“Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice.” — John 18:37
This is why we must be careful with one popular Christian assumption.
“My sheep hear My voice” does not mean every Christian is promised a continuous stream of individualized, extra-biblical sentences from Jesus.
God certainly can communicate however He chooses.
Scripture records dreams.
Visions.
Angelic messages.
Prophetic revelation.
Audible speech.
Providential guidance.
The Holy Spirit directing particular servants.
We should never reduce Almighty God to a formula and announce what He is incapable of doing.
But neither should we promise believers something the text itself does not promise.
And that distinction can rescue somebody from years of unnecessary spiritual anxiety.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for Jesus to speak while ignoring the place where He has unquestionably spoken.
Scripture.
The Bible is not God’s old voice.
It is not the spiritual equivalent of yesterday’s newspaper while Christians search for something newer and more exciting.
Jesus Himself repeatedly treated Scripture as authoritative.
When Satan tempted Him in the wilderness, Jesus answered:
“It is written.”
Again:
“It is written.”
Again:
“It is written.”
The incarnate Son of God did not treat written revelation as spiritually inferior.
Neither should we.
Paul writes:
The Greek word in 2 Timothy 3:16 is extraordinary:
θεόπνευστος — theopneustos.
It means “God-breathed.”
Scripture is God-breathed.
Paul continues that Scripture is profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
Think about that.
Some Christians desperately ask God for a word while their Bible remains closed.
They want direction but avoid doctrine.
They want whispers but resist commands.
They want revelation without repentance.
They want God to tell them whom to marry while ignoring what He already said about holiness.
They want God to reveal their destiny while refusing to forgive the person they hate.
They want God to confirm their dreams while avoiding Christ’s call to deny themselves.
And sometimes what we call “I can’t hear God” actually means:
“I don’t like what He has already said.”
That sentence hurts.
Because I have done it too.
It is easier to search for a mysterious spiritual impression than to obey a clear biblical command.
A mysterious voice might tell me something exciting.
Scripture might tell me to repent.
A mysterious voice might tell me I am entering my breakthrough season.
Scripture might tell me to forgive my enemy.
A mysterious voice might flatter my plans.
Scripture might crucify my pride.
And suddenly the real question becomes uncomfortable.
Do I want God to speak…
or do I want God to agree with me?
Because those are not the same thing.
This is where spiritual discernment becomes desperately important.
Not every thought in your head is God.
Not every coincidence is a divine instruction.
Not every powerful emotion is the Holy Spirit.
Not every dream is prophetic.
Not every open door means “go.”
Not every closed door means “stop.”
Not every person who says “God told me” was actually told something by God.
Human beings have desires.
Fears.
Memories.
Trauma.
Biases.
Imaginations.
Expectations.
And Scripture warns us that deception is real.
This is why John tells believers:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — 1 John 4:1
Notice that biblical faith does not demand gullibility.
It demands discernment.
Paul similarly writes:
Test.
Examine.
Hold fast to what is good.
Christian maturity is not believing every spiritual-sounding impression.
Christian maturity is increasingly learning to submit everything to the truth God has revealed.
So how does Jesus actually speak to His people?
First and foundationally, Christ addresses us through the Scriptures that testify about Him.
Jesus said of the Scriptures:
“They are they which testify of me.” — John 5:39
After His resurrection, on the road to Emmaus, Jesus did something astonishing.
Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He interpreted the Scriptures concerning Himself.
The Bible is not a collection of inspirational quotations centered on you.
Its great storyline leads us to Christ.
Creation.
Fall.
Promise.
Covenant.
Sacrifice.
Kingdom.
Prophecy.
Incarnation.
Cross.
Resurrection.
Church.
New creation.
Jesus stands at the center.
And when the Holy Spirit opens our understanding of Scripture, He does not lead us away from Christ into spiritual fascination with ourselves.
He glorifies Christ.
Jesus Himself said of the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me.” — John 16:14
That is an enormously important test.
Because there is a kind of spirituality that constantly talks about “God” while strangely making the individual the center of everything.
My destiny.
My promotion.
My breakthrough.
My enemies.
My prophetic word.
My season.
My blessing.
My platform.
My success.
But the Holy Spirit’s ministry is profoundly Christ-centered.
He convicts.
He teaches.
He reminds Christ’s disciples of Jesus’ words.
He glorifies the Son.
He forms Christlike fruit in believers.
So when you wonder whether something is from God, ask whether it agrees with Scripture and leads toward the character, truth, holiness, love, humility, and lordship of Jesus Christ.
God will never “lead” you to commit adultery.
God will never “tell” you to abandon biblical truth.
God will never “reveal” that Jesus is unnecessary.
God will never contradict His own holy character.
The Holy Spirit does not compete with the Word He inspired.
But what about impressions?
Convictions?
A strong sense that you should call someone?
An unexpected burden to pray?
A persistent thought about serving somewhere?
A circumstance that seems providential?
Christians from different theological traditions understand these experiences differently, and we should acknowledge that rather than pretending every faithful believer explains them identically.
Some Christians believe particular gifts of revelation continue today.
Others believe certain revelatory gifts belonged uniquely to the apostolic era.
Faithful Christians have debated these questions for generations.
But believers across those differences can affirm something crucial:
No personal impression has the authority of Scripture.
And no impression should be treated as permission to contradict Scripture.
This means humility should become part of our vocabulary.
Instead of carelessly saying,
“God told me you need to marry that person,”
perhaps we should sometimes say,
“I have a strong impression about this, but I could be wrong. Please test it against Scripture and seek wisdom.”
That sentence contains something desperately missing from much modern spirituality.
Humility.
Because claiming divine authority for our personal thoughts is serious.
If I say, “I think…”
you can disagree with me.
But if I say, “God told me…”
I have placed enormous pressure on your conscience.
I have effectively put God’s name behind my opinion.
That should make every Christian careful.
Especially pastors.
Teachers.
Parents.
Spouses.
Leaders.
Influencers.
Anyone with spiritual authority.
Never use “God told me” to control someone.
Never use Jesus’ name to manipulate another person into doing what you want.
Never weaponize supposed revelation.
The Shepherd does not need your manipulation to lead His sheep.
And perhaps someone reading this has been wounded precisely there.
Someone told you God said you had to stay.
Someone told you God said you had to give them money.
Someone told you questioning them meant questioning God.
Someone used spiritual language to control your choices.
And because you loved Jesus, you were afraid to resist.
Hear this carefully:
Biblical submission to Christ is not blind submission to every human being who claims divine authority.
Test what you are told.
Search the Scriptures.
Seek godly wisdom.
Look at fruit.
And keep Jesus—not a personality—at the center.
Because sheep ultimately belong to the Shepherd.
This also means something beautiful for the believer who feels spiritually numb.
Your relationship with Christ is not measured by how dramatic your spiritual experiences are.
Some days Scripture may pierce your heart.
Other days you may read a chapter and feel almost nothing.
Some prayers may leave you overwhelmed by God’s presence.
Others may feel like words hitting the ceiling.
Some worship services may bring tears.
Others may not.
Your emotions fluctuate.
Christ does not.
Your concentration fluctuates.
Christ does not.
Your spiritual intensity fluctuates.
Christ does not.
And look at what comes immediately after “My sheep hear My voice.”
Jesus says:
“And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” — John 10:28
Read that again.
The emphasis moves immediately toward Christ’s keeping power.
“I give…”
“They shall never perish…”
“No one will snatch them out of My hand.”
Then:
“My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand.” — John 10:29
You may have arrived at John 10 terrified because you wondered whether you were holding tightly enough to Jesus.
And Jesus turns the picture around.
The Shepherd is holding His sheep.
That does not make obedience irrelevant.
Jesus explicitly says His sheep follow Him.
But our hope is not finally located in the perfection of our grip.
It is located in the faithfulness of Christ.
And that is where this becomes deeply personal.
Because maybe you have followed strange voices.
Maybe the voice was money.
Maybe approval.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe success.
Maybe religion without Christ.
Maybe your own wounded heart.
Maybe somebody told you that you would finally be valuable if enough people admired you.
So you followed.
And followed.
And followed.
Until one day you looked around and realized you had wandered farther than you ever intended.
Sin always has a voice.
It promises before it destroys.
“Just once.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You deserve this.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“This will finally satisfy you.”
“You are too far gone anyway.”
Then after you fall, the voice changes.
“Look at you.”
“God could never want you now.”
“You knew better.”
“Hide.”
“Pretend.”
“Run.”
That is one of sin’s cruelest tricks.
Temptation says, “Come closer.”
Shame says, “Never go home.”
But the Gospel tells another story.
There is a Shepherd who came for sinners.
Jesus did not come for people who had successfully repaired themselves.
He came to seek and save the lost.
At the cross, the Good Shepherd became the Lamb who was slain.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with your sin through the blood of His Son.
Repentance, therefore, is not payment for grace.
It is the sinner turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because an algorithm happened to place another Christian article on your screen.
But because somewhere beneath your exhaustion, compromise, questions, disappointment, religious performance, or secret shame…
you still want Jesus.
Maybe faintly.
Maybe desperately.
Maybe you do not even know what you want anymore.
But something inside you knows that running has not healed you.
Hiding has not healed you.
Pretending has not healed you.
And perhaps the Shepherd’s words are confronting you again:
“Follow me.”
Not:
“Fix everything first.”
Not:
“Become impressive.”
Not:
“Make yourself worthy.”
Follow Me.
Bring the sin into the light.
Bring the questions.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the addiction you keep promising you will defeat alone.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the secret browser history.
Bring the pride.
Bring the church hurt.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
Jesus already knows His sheep.
“I know them.”
Those words can sound frightening until you realize who is speaking them.
The Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
He knows.
And still He calls.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Grace that finds sinners where they are and refuses to leave them unchanged.
The Gospel does not say your sin is harmless.
It says Christ is mighty to save.
The Gospel does not tell you to celebrate your chains.
It announces that Jesus came to break the dominion of sin.
The Gospel does not tell you to manufacture a better identity.
It calls you to die and rise with Christ.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So tomorrow morning, when you wonder how to “hear God,” do not begin by trying to empty your mind until a mysterious sentence appears.
Open Scripture.
Read slowly.
Read in context.
Ask what the author actually meant.
Ask what the passage reveals about God.
Ask how it points toward Christ and fits within the whole counsel of Scripture.
Pray for the Holy Spirit to illuminate your understanding and transform your heart.
Then obey what is clear.
When Scripture commands forgiveness, forgive.
When Scripture exposes sexual immorality, flee it.
When Scripture commands love, love.
When Scripture calls you to repentance, repent.
When Scripture tells you to pray, pray.
When Scripture tells you to gather with believers, do not isolate yourself indefinitely.
When Scripture tells you Christ is sufficient, stop searching for another savior.
And when circumstances, impressions, advice, desires, dreams, opportunities, or internal thoughts seem to be leading you somewhere, test them.
Never make the Bible say what it does not say.
Never confuse your desires with God’s decrees.
Seek wisdom.
Pray.
Listen to mature believers.
Examine your motives.
Watch the fruit.
And where Scripture has given freedom, do not become paralyzed waiting for a supernatural sign God never promised to provide.
Sometimes wisdom looks remarkably ordinary.
Pray.
Think.
Seek counsel.
Make the wisest faithful decision you can.
Trust God.
Walk.
Because the Christian life is not primarily about decoding secret messages.
It is about knowing and following Jesus.
And perhaps this article exposed something you have never admitted.
Maybe you have been chasing voices while neglecting the Word.
Maybe you have been following a preacher more closely than Christ.
Maybe somebody’s “prophetic word” has controlled your life for years.
Maybe you have mistaken anxiety for God’s voice.
Maybe you have been terrified that God abandoned you because you do not experience Him the way somebody else claims to.
Or maybe you know exactly what Christ has already commanded…
and you have simply refused to follow.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Do not turn the comment section into a stage for pretending everybody is strong.
Let it become a place where people remember they are not the only ones fighting.
And somebody you know may desperately need this truth.
Maybe even share it for the person who does not yet believe, because the center of this message is not a technique for hearing supernatural voices.
It is Jesus Christ.
There will probably come another night when emotions become louder than truth.
Come back then.
Read John 10 again.
Remember the Shepherd.

Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, faithfully, and for God’s glory—not as a transaction for blessing, not as a way of purchasing God’s favor, and never as a substitute for belonging to and giving faithfully through your local church.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be earned.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9
Your greatest need is not membership in a platform.
Your greatest need is Christ.
So hear the Shepherd where He has truly spoken.
Trust what He has revealed.
Test every other voice.
Repent when His Word exposes you.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Jesus.
And when your feelings scream that you are abandoned, remember the words surrounding the verse that once frightened you:
“My sheep hear my voice…”
“I know them…”
“They follow me…”
“I give unto them eternal life…”
“They shall never perish…”
“No one will snatch them out of My hand.”
Maybe you thought Christianity depended on whether you could hear Jesus loudly enough.
But perhaps John 10 has been telling you something better all along.
The miracle is not merely that the sheep recognize the Shepherd.
The miracle is that the Shepherd knows their names, laid down His life for them, rose from the grave—and still calls wandering sheep home.
Share that truth.
Because somewhere tonight, another sheep is listening through a storm of voices…
and desperately needs to remember which Shepherd died to bring them home.
